title: How Routine Rules Can Create Systemic Inequities
audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers
filename: courses/One DSD - F22 - How Routine Rules Can Create Systemic Inequities.pptx

slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
How Routine Rules Can Create Systemic Inequities
Trace how connected requirements, handoffs, information, and authority can repeatedly shape access and opportunity.
Foundation self-directed learning
slides.narration: A rule can appear reasonable when examined alone and still contribute to difficulty in a connected process. People experience the whole pathway, including the transitions between offices or tasks. This course follows service, development, and community examples to examine those connections. It continues Equity in Policy and Legislative Practice by introducing possible mechanisms rather than announcing findings. You will map a burden, compare a response, and identify the evidence and relevant responsibilities needed to understand whether the proposed explanation fits.

slides.text:
A reasonable step meets another reasonable step
One notice requires a document by a deadline. Another office needs time to supply it and uses a different document name.

The combined task may be harder than either instruction suggests.

Which connection would you inspect before blaming the person for a late response?
slides.narration: Each office may describe its own instruction accurately. The person still has to recognize the document, obtain it, and submit it in time. A mismatch between names can use part of the response window before the document is requested. Repetition could make the same delay recur even when nobody intended it. The opening reflection asks you to locate the connection, not assume it explains every late response. Evidence about arrival, requests, timing, and the person’s experience would clarify the pathway.

slides.text:
A system is a set of connected choices
Rules, resources, information, tasks, and decisions connect to form a process.

Systemic inequity concerns recurring conditions that unevenly restrict opportunity or distribute burden.

A possible mechanism explains how an effect could arise; it still needs evidence.
slides.narration: Systemic does not mean that every person in the organization shares the same intent. It directs attention toward arrangements that repeatedly shape experience. A requirement, handoff, and resource assumption can combine in a way no single step reveals. Describe the relevant boundary and connection rather than treating the whole agency as one explanation. Unequal results can prompt inquiry, but they do not establish a cause by themselves. The learning examples help identify a mechanism and the evidence that would test it.

slides.text:
The document name uses part of the response window
A notice requests a “verification summary.” The supplying office calls it a “confirmation letter.” Clarification takes time before the person can respond.

If repeated, the mismatch may delay people without insider knowledge.

Examine names, timing, and the handoff rather than only the final response.
slides.narration: The person’s task crosses an organizational boundary. Staff at the final step may see only that the response arrived late, while the earlier naming confusion remains absent from the record. A clearer name and handoff could help, but other conditions may also matter. The next case asks how to examine that sequence without assuming one repair settles every delay. The fiction supplies a plausible pathway, not a measured rate, a current policy requirement, or a conclusion about the person’s effort.

slides.text:
A document mismatch before a deadline
A notice requests a “verification summary.” The supplying office calls it a “confirmation letter.” Clarification uses part of the response window. What response best examines the pathway?
A. Judge the person’s effort from the final late response alone.
B. Examine naming, timing, and the handoff with relevant evidence and responsibilities.
C. Guarantee that one wording repair will prevent every later delay.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The notice and supplying office may each be clear to staff who know the terminology. The person using both has a different task. Consider how clarification, document production, and submission connect, and which responsibility governs each choice. The case establishes a possible pathway but does not explain every late response. Compare a response that investigates the sequence with one that judges the person or guarantees a repair. You can identify a useful next inquiry without assuming all requirements are changeable or that one edit will produce a complete access result.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Judge the person’s effort from the final late response alone.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Examine naming, timing, and the handoff with relevant evidence and responsibilities.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Guarantee that one wording repair will prevent every later delay.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The final result omits earlier conditions. Repeating that judgment can turn a process mismatch into a person label. Trace the sequence and hear the relevant account; effort and the cause of all delay remain unknown.

Which arrow in this pathway needs evidence before you claim a cause?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The final response alone cannot show what occurred before submission. Treating lateness as a verdict about effort may hide the naming and timing conditions. If repeated, that account can preserve the mismatch while people receive the blame. Examine the sequence with appropriate evidence and perspectives. The case leaves other causes, actual effort, and the wider frequency unknown.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This makes the connected burden available for review. Repeated mismatch may favor insider knowledge. Check the evidence and actual requirements; the best repair and wider effects are not yet established.

Which arrow in this pathway needs evidence before you claim a cause?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The response identifies where an internal mismatch may affect the person’s task. Relevant offices can consider the names, turnaround, and requirements while people using the route explain the combined experience. This may support a focused repair. The inquiry still needs evidence for each link and the appropriate authority. It is not a finding that the mismatch caused every delay or that a particular change is approved.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A naming repair may help while timing or other barriers remain. Repeating a universal guarantee can conceal unfinished work. Examine the full route and actual effects; one proposal does not settle every delay.

Which arrow in this pathway needs evidence before you claim a cause?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Consistent naming may reduce confusion, but a remaining timing conflict or inaccessible route could still delay the task. A universal guarantee would make the repair appear more complete than the evidence allows. Trace the revised sequence and check appropriate effects. The fiction supplies a naming concern, not a tested repair or proof that every future response will be timely.

slides.text:
Locate who can change which part
A person seeing the difficulty may not control the notice, supplying office, or response rule.

Identify the actual responsibility for the relevant choice.

A clear account can connect expertise without assigning one staff member authority over the whole process.
slides.narration: Authority is distributed through the organization. Communication staff may understand the notice, another area may know document production, and the service program may control the response requirements. People using the route hold knowledge about the combined task. The learning does not assign these roles to actual offices; it shows why the specific responsibility needs clarification. A proposed response should reach the relevant decision rather than promise a change no one present can make. Coordination is useful when it keeps the whole experience visible.

slides.text:
Small burdens may accumulate
A confusing term can lead to a call, a wait, another visit, and less time to complete the next step.

Time, transport, language, digital access, and prior knowledge can change the burden.

Ask which link is supported rather than assuming everyone experiences the sequence alike.
slides.narration: Several modest demands can become a substantial task when they occur together. A person with available time and institutional familiarity may resolve a confusing term quickly, while another person needs a different route or support. Those circumstances should be examined, not inferred from identity. Trace the practical links and ask what information supports them. If repeated, the pathway may place extra effort on the same people. A map identifies the possible accumulation without establishing how common it is or which cause dominates.

slides.text:
An internal choice travels into daily life
A definition becomes a form, an instruction, a request, or a review criterion.

Its practical effect may occur far from the drafting room.

Ask what the person must do and which resources the sequence assumes.
slides.narration: Public power often appears through ordinary internal decisions rather than a dramatic announcement. A field added to a form can become another document to obtain. A definition can change how a request is recorded. The staff member may be solving a legitimate administrative need while the person encounters a new task. Follow the relevant trip and examine the assumptions it carries. This is attention to impact, not an accusation about motive. The specific effect still needs evidence and the appropriate decision context.

slides.text:
Routine can make a shortcut feel inevitable
A familiar route may be repeated because each office’s part appears settled.

Ask where the arrangement came from and whether the purpose requires that exact method.

A real requirement and a customary implementation choice are not always the same.
slides.narration: The word “always” can conceal a question that has not recently been examined. Some choices may be required, while others are habits developed under earlier conditions. Identify the actual source and responsibility before proposing to remove anything. A changeable format or naming choice may be enough to address one problem, while a response rule requires a different review. Repeating the route because it is familiar can preserve a burden. The course does not determine which requirements are legally changeable in a real situation.

slides.text:
Opportunity that depends on prior opportunity
A development path uses informal notice, manager nomination, and prior high-visibility work.

People missing the first invitation may be less likely to gain experience used in the next selection.

Examine the criteria and connected opportunities before deciding why outcomes differ.
slides.narration: The steps can reinforce one another. An informal invitation may limit who learns about an assignment, and the assignment may later count as experience for another opportunity. Each criterion might have a useful purpose, yet the combined path deserves examination. The next choice asks how to trace the loop without lowering relevant standards or claiming every selection is biased. The fiction does not supply actual employees, nomination reasons, or outcome data. It identifies a possible connection between earlier access and later consideration.

slides.text:
Experience selected by an earlier invitation
A development route uses informal notice, manager nomination, and prior high-visibility work. People outside the first invitation may lack experience used in the next selection. What should be examined?
A. The connected opportunity route and relevant criteria, without assuming why every selection occurred.
B. Only the final experience criterion, treating earlier access as irrelevant.
C. All experience standards should be removed immediately.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: Relevant experience can be important, and the case does not tell you to disregard it. The equity question also asks how people gain the experience that later counts. A narrow invitation route could influence who reaches visible work and then who is considered again. Examine the actual criteria and opportunities together. No personnel records, nomination motives, or measured selection outcomes are supplied. The strongest response identifies the possible loop while retaining evidence, appropriate responsibilities, and the distinction between improving access to a standard and removing the standard itself.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. The connected opportunity route and relevant criteria, without assuming why every selection occurred.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Only the final experience criterion, treating earlier access as irrelevant.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. All experience standards should be removed immediately.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This examines how access to experience can shape later consideration. It may reveal a repeated opportunity loop. Retain work standards and suitable evidence; actual selection causes and the best response remain unknown.

Where could the opportunity loop begin before the final selection?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A connected review asks how the criterion and the route to meeting it work together. Informal notice may matter, or other conditions may explain the pattern. Suitable evidence and the employee’s chosen account can clarify that without assuming motives. If the loop is supported, an appropriate response can examine opportunity access while preserving relevant standards. The case does not establish a final finding or approved change.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The final criterion may depend on an earlier route. Repeating a narrow review can keep that loop invisible. Examine how relevant experience becomes available; fairness is not established by the criterion alone.

Where could the opportunity loop begin before the final selection?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Examining only the last criterion can make the earlier opportunity route disappear. If the same people repeatedly gain experience through a narrow invitation network, the final selection may reproduce that distribution while looking independent. Follow the actual connection and test the explanation. The case does not prove that experience is an improper criterion or that every choice was unequal; it shows why the earlier route matters.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Experience may serve a legitimate work purpose. Removing it without inquiry can undermine the task. Examine criteria and routes to meet them through actual responsibilities; this fiction supplies no approval to change standards.

Where could the opportunity loop begin before the final selection?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: An experience standard can be relevant to the work. Removing every standard would answer a different question and could undermine a legitimate purpose. Examine whether the criterion fits and whether people have realistic ways to gain the relevant experience. Actual authority and processes remain. The learning identifies a possible loop, not approval to change selection criteria or a finding that no experience requirement is justified.

slides.text:
A feedback loop can preserve the familiar
People who receive visible work gain experience that may make them more likely to receive the next visible assignment.

The pattern can grow even without a new explicit exclusion at every step.

Ask whether the experience criterion fits the task and how people can gain relevant experience.
slides.narration: Experience can be a legitimate criterion. The equity question also concerns how people become able to meet it. If the route to experience is narrow, repeating the criterion may reinforce the same distribution of opportunity. Examine the actual task, available development routes, and evidence of selection. Do not assume that every familiar choice is improper or that experience should be ignored. A useful inquiry keeps standards and access connected, with the explanation open to information that supports or challenges the proposed loop.

slides.text:
Access to experience can shape later opportunity
Proposed relationship for practice
1. Learn about visible assignment
2. Gain relevant experience
3. Meet later experience criterion
4. Receive another opportunity
What evidence would clarify whether the first invitation shapes later opportunity?
A legitimate criterion can interact with a narrow route to meet it.
slides.narration:
PRACTICE EXAMPLE: Original employee development pathway in F22.

A legitimate criterion can interact with a narrow route to meet it.

What evidence would clarify whether the first invitation shapes later opportunity?

No actual personnel outcome, cause, or approved change is represented.

slides.text:
The life cycle connects different gates
Recruitment, onboarding, assignments, development, and advancement can carry information from earlier decisions.

A label or missing opportunity may travel forward.

Follow the relevant connection; do not treat one observation as the whole employee history.
slides.narration: An early judgment can be reused later without its original context. A note about a format difficulty might become a broad assumption about ability, or a missed invitation might become a lack of experience. The employee life-cycle perspective helps identify that travel. Ask which decisions actually rely on the earlier information and whether the account remains accurate. This is a possible mechanism to examine through appropriate responsibilities. The course supplies no personnel evidence or permission to collect private records for a learning exercise.

slides.text:
Hear the pathway from the people using it
Community accounts can reveal steps and burdens staff records omit.

Briefs prepare questions about history and institutional experience; they do not prove a cause.

Invite varied perspectives through usable routes and preserve the scope of each account.
slides.narration: A person may explain that a response failed before it entered the official record. That information can reveal a part of the pathway staff would otherwise miss. A brief may prepare attention to trust or communication conditions while the actual account identifies the task. Avoid asking one person to explain everyone’s experience. Repeatedly using only successful participants as the source may leave the earlier barrier invisible. The inquiry should combine suitable process evidence and varied accounts without claiming the group’s whole experience is known.

slides.text:
Compare repairs across the sequence
Consistent naming can address one confusion; a clearer handoff may address another.

A new route can also move effort, delay, or dependency elsewhere.

Trace each option through the whole task and retain actual requirements and responsibility.
slides.narration: A repair should be evaluated against the mechanism it is meant to address. A clearer term may help identify the document while leaving a timing conflict unchanged. An assisted route may solve one submission problem while requiring an additional appointment. Explain those tradeoffs without assuming the largest redesign is best. The current arrangement also needs evidence. A conditional recommendation can be useful when information or authority remains open, and it should not guarantee every person’s completion or a wider equity result.

slides.text:
A community response is missing from the count
A participant tried a contact route, received an unclear document request, and never reached registration. The summary counts only registered people.

Their account may reveal an earlier filter.

Examine that step without treating one account as every absence’s explanation.
slides.narration: The summary can be accurate about registered participants and incomplete about the route into registration. The person’s account identifies a possible point where the process lost them. If the same route is used repeatedly, people facing that difficulty may remain absent from the information used to review it. The next case asks how to keep the count and experience distinct. The fiction supplies no prevalence, group cause, or approved repair; it supports a focused question about the earlier step.

slides.text:
Who never reaches the participation count?
A participant cannot complete an unclear document request and never reaches registration. The report counts only registered people. What is the most careful next inquiry?
A. Treat the report as proof that everyone could use the route.
B. Claim this one account explains every missing participant.
C. Examine the earlier step and the report’s boundary, using appropriate evidence and varied accounts.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The registered-participant report may be accurate about what it counts. Its boundary does not include everyone who attempted the earlier task. The person’s account supplies information about that missing step, which can inform a focused review. A community brief may prepare questions about institutional context but cannot establish the cause. Compare responses that preserve both the record and the account with responses that overstate either. The case supplies no population rate, broad community finding, or tested alternative, so a careful next inquiry should keep those questions open.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Treat the report as proof that everyone could use the route.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Claim this one account explains every missing participant.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Examine the earlier step and the report’s boundary, using appropriate evidence and varied accounts.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The count describes registered people, not everyone who tried to reach registration. Repeating that conclusion can hide an earlier gate. Examine the route and population; universal access is not established.

What experience is outside the report’s counted population?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Accuracy within a count is different from completeness about access. People who could not register may be absent from the report’s population. Treating the count as proof that everyone could use the route can repeatedly hide that earlier filter. Examine the registration path and relevant evidence. The report still has value for its stated population, but it does not establish universal participation or explain missing people.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
One account identifies a concern without proving every absence’s cause. Repeating that inference may misdirect repair. Keep the scope clear and seek relevant evidence; the wider pattern remains unknown.

What experience is outside the report’s counted population?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The account can make a concern visible without explaining all absences. Other people may encounter different conditions or have different reasons not to participate. Expanding the account into a universal cause may lead to an unsuitable repair. Preserve its scope and seek appropriate process evidence and varied perspectives. The learning does not supply prevalence, a complete explanation, or a finding about any real community.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This connects the person’s account with what the report omits. It may reveal a recurring filter before registration. Examine suitable records and perspectives; prevalence, cause, and the eventual repair are still open.

What experience is outside the report’s counted population?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This response uses the two sources for the questions they can answer. The report describes registered participants; the account identifies an earlier difficulty. Together they can support a focused inquiry into a possible filter without proving how common it is. Appropriate records and other perspectives may clarify the pathway. No completed causal finding, approved alternative, or improved participation result is supplied by the fiction.

slides.text:
A map shows a hypothesis, not a finding
An arrow can describe a possible connection without proving that one step caused the next.

Ask what evidence supports each link and what alternative explanation remains.

Keep unknown information visible rather than drawing certainty into the diagram.
slides.narration: Process maps are powerful because they make a connection easy to see. That clarity can also make an untested explanation look settled. Mark the sequence as an observed or proposed pathway, and explain what the arrows mean. Timing, different resources, or another step may change the account. Ask what evidence would clarify the link. A map should help people inspect reasoning, not turn a plausible narrative into proof. The visual can remain useful while the causal question is still open.

slides.text:
Repetition matters, but frequency needs evidence
One account can identify a concern worth examining.

To describe a recurring pattern, consider suitable records, definitions, periods, and varied perspectives.

Do not dismiss a single concern or invent prevalence from it.
slides.narration: A barrier does not need to be common to deserve attention in a particular situation. Claims about a recurring system-wide pattern require different evidence from claims about one person’s task. Distinguish those scopes. Appropriate information may show repetition, variation, or another explanation. Missing records may also limit what can be known. Avoid using the absence of a tally as a reason to ignore the account, and avoid turning the account into an unsupported rate. The next inquiry should fit the question actually being asked.

slides.text:
Map one pathway in your own words
Use the document, development, or registration fiction.

Write three connected steps, a possible accumulating burden, and the evidence needed to examine one link.

Identify the relevant decision without assigning unestablished authority.
slides.narration: You do not need a complete agency diagram to practice systems thinking. Select the sequence that explains the concern: recognizing the document, requesting it, and submitting it is enough for one focused map. In the development case, notice how invitation and experience connect. Explain which link is known and which is proposed. Your reflection can remain private and use only the fiction. The exercise prepares a clearer account for appropriate analysis rather than instructing you to change an actual requirement or inspect personnel records.

slides.text:
A later improvement does not settle every cause
A naming repair and a later increase in completed responses are different pieces of evidence.

Ask whether other conditions changed and whether the comparison fits.

A useful action can be recognized while its causal effect and remaining barriers stay open.
slides.narration: Suppose the offices adopt one document name and the next period has more completed responses. The change in naming is implementation evidence. The later count is outcome information, but timing, outreach, staffing, or other conditions may also differ. A before-and-after sequence does not establish the cause by itself. Ask what the evidence can support and what further review is appropriate. This distinction preserves the value of a repair without claiming every improvement or every person’s experience was produced by it.

slides.text:
See the connection before closing the question
Routine rules can distribute burden through the way they connect, repeat, and influence later decisions.

Describe the mechanism, relevant authority, evidence, and unresolved questions plainly.

Continue into evidence and goal-planning learning in the policy sequence.
slides.narration: Systems thinking helps you examine a task from the perspective of people moving through it. The cases connect document names and timing, opportunity and prior experience, and registration with missing accounts. None supplies a complete finding about an actual unit or program. They show why purpose, authority, and evidence belong alongside practical experience. A clearer map can support a focused next inquiry. Continued learning helps distinguish what a process does, what it may cause, and what an appropriate response still needs to establish.

outcomes: Explain systemic inequity through connected rules, information, authority, and recurring effects.
Trace how an internal decision travels through a public-service process.
Recognize when several small burdens may accumulate for the same people.
Identify a possible mechanism and the evidence needed to examine it.
